Ecologic (aggregate) effect estimates are inevitably used as individual-effect estimates, yet ecologic variation in individual-effect distributions biases contextual estimates—plausibly common, since social context is not randomized across administrative regions. Ecologic data provide only marginal observations on the joint distribution of individually defined confounders and outcomes, identifying neither contextual nor individual-level effects. Multilevel designs using individual and group-level data address these problems but still share issues of inappropriate aggregation and temporal covariate change.

Separately, trisomic and monosomic (aneuploid) embryos account for at least 10% of human pregnancies, exceeding 50% for women nearing the end of reproductive lifespan. Errors almost always occur in the oocyte, but their molecular basis remains elusive; human and model-organism studies indicate the age-related rise in female meiotic errors stems from interplay between unique oogenesis features and endogenous and exogenous factors—not a single factor.
